newsitem.title: USA: Democrats take tough line to free chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Democrats take tough line to free chemical treaty.

text.p: Democrats will hold up all Senate business to try to force majority Republicans to set a date for debate on a treaty outlawing chemical weapons worldwide, their leader said on Wednesday.
"I think it's the only leverage we've got," Democratic Leader Tom Daschle told reporters.

The United States must ratify the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention before it comes into force on April 29 or it will have no voice in implementing it. The treaty, which bans the production, stockpiling and use of poison gases, remains bottled up by Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms while time runs out for debate.
Congress takes a two-week recess starting on Monday, leaving less than three weeks for debate and a vote. A two-thirds Senate majority is needed for approval.
One major piece of business expected before the recess is a compromise resolution being drafted expressing congressional dissatisfaction with Mexico's performance in the war against illegal drugs.

"We're determined to get a date for the Chemical Weapons Convention and unless we get some sort of date we're not going to be inclined to move any additional legislation on Mexico this week," Daschle told reporters. He said he had informed the White House of the planned tactic.
Under Senate rules, unanimous consent is required for most actions, meaning Democrats can hold up any debate, including on a motion to adjourn.

Helms, a North Carolina Republican who has long been a foe of the arms treaty, has called for a series of conditions to Senate approval and has demanded administration concessions on other issues as a price for action on the treaty.

Administration officials have talked to some senators to try to meet some of the objections without dealing a fatal blow to U.S. participation in the pact. Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said progress had been made and it was possible the treaty could reach the floor after the recess.
"I am working aggressively to address concerns on all sides of this issue," he said. "We are talking."

He told a reporter earlier: "Of course you have to work with the chairman (Helms). And I told them (administration officials) again yesterday, 'If you think you can roll the chairman, you'd better bring your lunch.'"
The administration counters opposition to the treaty by pointing out that the United States is already committed to destroying its chemical weapons.

"The bottom line is, do we really want to keep the world safe for other people's poison gas, and I hope those realities will shape the Senate's thinking as we proceed to the April 29th deadline," Arms Control and Disarmament Agency director John Holum told a State Department briefing on Wednesday.
